The prevalence of rOSA after AT varied widely, ranging from 18.6% to 85.0%, depending on assessment criteria, study population and duration, patients’ characteristics, and the timing of postoperative follow–up. Among the identified predictors, obesity was the most consistently reported risk factor. Nine studies that analyzed body mass index (BMI) found that children with obesity had markedly higher rates of rOSA, with prevalence ranging from 23.0% to 72.8% [ 1 , 9 , 10 , 14 , 20 , 22 , 23 , 25 ]. One study evaluated OSA prevalence on the first postoperative night and reported a rate of 85.0% among obese children, reflecting immediate postoperative findings [ 13 ]. Age was also identified as a factor associated with postoperative outcomes. Several studies reported that older children were more likely to experience rOSA. However, reported prevalence estimates varied widely across studies and should not be interpreted as age-specific rates [ 1 , 22 , 23 , 25 ]. Four different studies highlighted asthma as a condition linked with poorer post–AT improvement, especially when coexisting with obesity or more severe OSA before surgery [ 1 , 10 , 20 , 22 ]. However, statistical adjustment for confounding factors varied across studies. Children with DS also showed a high prevalence of rOSA—typically between 54.0% and 68.0%—even though most showed a measurable reduction in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) after AT [ 24 , 26 , 27 ]. However, effect estimates and multivariable adjustment were inconsistently reported. Other contributing factors included craniofacial or developmental abnormalities, reported in some studies with rOSA rates between 38.0% and 84.6%, as well as a higher preoperative AHI, which repeatedly appeared as a strong predictor of persistent symptoms [ 1 , 9 , 10 , 21 , 22 ]. In addition to clinical characteristics, one study highlighted the role of social and environmental influences, such as exposure to tobacco smoke, lower maternal education, or racial and socioeconomic disparities, which were associated with less favorable post–AT outcomes [ 20 ]. 4. Discussion OSA in children remains one of the most frequent and clinically relevant sleep–related breathing disorder. While AT is widely recognized as the first–line treatment for pediatric OSA, up to 40% of children may continue to exhibit rOSA after surgery [ 1 , 3 , 8 , 9 ]. The continued presence of OSA following surgical intervention underscores its complex and multifactorial pathophysiology, encompassing anatomical, metabolic, inflammatory, genetic, and social determinants. Obesity is consistently identified as one of the most frequently reported predictors of residual disease after AT. Several studies have confirmed that obese children are significantly more likely to have persistent OSA compared to their normal–weight peers [ 6 , 13 , 14 , 15 ]. De et al. reported that 85% of obese children continued to exhibit OSA on the first postoperative night [ 13 ]. Importantly, subsequent studies indicate that this persistence is not limited to the immediate postoperative period. Bhattacharjee et al. demonstrated that obesity, particularly when combined with older age and chronic asthma, was strongly associated with rOSA in the longer term, with a prevalence of 72.8% [ 1 ]. Consistent with these findings, Hsu et al. observed that although surgical intervention resulted in symptomatic improvement across all weight categories, obese children remained at a significantly higher risk of persistent OSA over time [ 14 ]. Recent studies suggest that obesity contributes not only through mechanical airway narrowing but also via increased systemic inflammation and altered neuromuscular control [ 2 , 28 ]. In addition, untreated OSA has been associated with metabolic and endocrine dysfunction mediated by inflammatory and neuroendocrine mechanisms, supporting a bidirectional relationship between OSA and obesity [ 11 ]. Taken together, these findings indicate that obesity represents one of the most important risk factors for the development and persistence of OSA. Accordingly, current evidence suggests that weight reduction and lifestyle modification constitute essential components of postoperative management, as even modest weight loss following AT can significantly reduce apnea severity and decrease the likelihood of persistent or recurrent OSA in obese pediatric patients [ 6 , 12 , 15 , 16 , 17 ]. In our results, age appears to be a significant determinant of rOSA after AT. Older age has been consistently associated with an increased risk of rOSA following AT, suggesting that age itself may represent an independent risk factor [ 1 , 22 , 23 , 25 ]. Potential contributing mechanisms include progressive airway remodeling and age–related changes in upper airway function, while obesity may further exacerbate this risk in older children [ 1 ]. Consistent with these findings, Alonso–Álvarez et al. identified age, obesity, and higher baseline respiratory disturbance index as independent predictors of poorer treatment response [ 23 ]. Notably, younger obese children tend to achieve higher cure rates and greater improvements in obstructive AHI than their older counterparts, suggesting that age modifies the influence of obesity on treatment outcomes [ 25 ]. At the younger end of the age spectrum, rOSA has also been reported, particularly among children with severe preoperative disease or relevant comorbidities. Nath et al. observed that very young children (<3 years) with severe preoperative OSA frequently exhibited residual disease following AT [ 22 ]. These finding consistent with the European Respiratory Society statement by Kaditis et al., which emphasizes that young children with comorbidities or severe baseline OSA remain at increased risk of postoperative residual disease [ 29 ]. Overall, both very young children and older children appear to be at heightened risk of suboptimal response to AT. However, the underlying mechanisms may differ, with developmental airway factors predominating in younger children and structural or metabolic factors playing a more prominent role in older children. Asthma is another frequently reported risk factor for rOSA. Both conditions share similar inflammatory pathways, including eosinophilic infiltration, airway hyperreactivity, and nocturnal hypoxemia [ 28 , 30 ]. Bhattacharjee et al. identified chronic asthma as an independent predictor of postoperative OSA, particularly when combined with obesity or severe baseline disease [ 1 ]. Imanguli et al. also reported that asthmatic children had higher residual AHI and poorer postoperative outcomes [ 10 ]. These associations may be explained by chronic upper airway inflammation and mucosal edema, which increase pharyngeal collapsibility during sleep [ 28 , 30 ]. However, poorly controlled asthma remains a significant risk factor for persistent OSA, highlighting the need for integrated management of both conditions [ 5 ]. OSA and allergic diseases are commonly co–occurring respiratory conditions in children, and their interrelationship has been widely and frequently discussed in the scientific literature. Given the close interaction between the upper and lower airways, attention should also be paid to the high prevalence of allergic rhinitis (AR) in children with asthma [ 31 , 32 ]. AR and asthma frequently coexist as part of the “united airway” concept, and many asthmatic patients have either undiagnosed or suboptimally controlled rhinitis [ 31 , 32 ]. Chronic nasal obstruction and increased airway resistance associated with AR can further promote adenoid hypertrophy, mouth breathing and destabilize upper airway patency during sleep, thereby contributing to rOSA risk [ 33 ]. Consequently, inadequate recognition or treatment of AR may partially underlie the poorer postoperative outcomes observed in children with asthma, underscoring the importance of evaluating and managing AR in this population [ 34 ]. Children with DS represent one of the highest–risk populations for residual and recurrent OSA after AT. Multiple studies have documented rOSA rates ranging from 50% to 70% in this group [ 24 , 26 , 27 , 35 ]. Senthilvel et al. found that although AHI significantly improved after surgery, 54% of DS patients continued to experience moderate–to–severe OSA [ 24 ]. Tanner et al. reported similar findings and noted that these children often require additional airway management strategies beyond surgery [ 26 ]. The persistence of OSA in DS is largely attributed to characteristic craniofacial morphology, including midfacial hypoplasia, macroglossia, narrowed nasopharyngeal lumen, and pharyngeal hypotonia [ 27 , 35 ]. Furthermore, the high prevalence of obesity in this population exacerbates upper airway obstruction [ 36 ]. These findings highlight the importance of early postoperative monitoring, follow–up sleep evaluation, and timely consideration of adjunctive therapies, including continuous positive airway pressure or other treatment modalities. In our systematic review, craniofacial features emerged as important determinants of postoperative outcomes following AT. Maeda et al. reported that 84.6% of children with mandibular hypoplasia continued to exhibit OSA after surgery, with smaller mandibular dimensions correlating with higher postoperative AHI values [ 21 ]. Similarly, Imanguli et al. identified craniofacial and neurological abnormalities as significant risk factors for rOSA [ 10 ]. These clinical observations are supported by recent cephalometric and three–dimensional imaging studies, which have consistently demonstrated that mandibular retrusion, increased lower facial height, and reduced upper airway dimensions are key structural contributors to pediatric OSA [ 18 , 19 ]. Collectively, these findings suggest that preoperative assessment of craniofacial anatomy may contribute to more informed surgical decision–making and potentially improved long–term outcomes. Beyond clinical and anatomical factors, socioeconomic and environmental determinants also play a meaningful role. Fayson et al. demonstrated that Black children from socioeconomically disadvantaged neighborhoods were more likely to have rOSA after AT, independent of obesity or preoperative AHI [ 20 ]. Similar findings were reported by Wang et al., who found that lower income, maternal education level, and exposure to household smoke were associated with higher postoperative AHI [ 37 ]. These disparities may reflect differences in healthcare access, environmental exposures, and adherence to postoperative follow–up [ 37 ]. In addition, secondhand smoke and indoor air pollutants may promote airway inflammation, further increasing the risk of persistent OSA symptoms [ 3 , 38 ]. Overall, these findings underscore the contribution of social and environmental contexts to residual disease and highlight the importance of addressing modifiable non–clinical factors in the comprehensive management of pediatric OSA. This review has several limitations that should be acknowledged. The literature search was conducted in PubMed and the Cochrane Library, both of which provide extensive coverage of peer-reviewed biomedical and clinical research, including the majority of high-impact journals in sleep medicine. However, restricting the search to these databases may have introduced a degree of selection bias, as studies indexed exclusively in other databases or available as grey literature might not have been identified. Conference abstracts, trial registries, and direct author contact were not systematically pursued. In addition, only English-language articles were included. Another limitation is that only a small proportion of the children included in the reviewed studies were younger than three years of age. Therefore, this population subgroup may not be fully represented. Nevertheless, AT is rarely performed in this age group. Several of the included studies were of limited sample size and the results should be interpreted cautiously, particularly the one evaluating abnormal maxillofacial morphology as a potential risk factor. Furthermore, substantial variability was observed in the timing of postoperative PSG reassessment. In some studies, PSG was conducted more than one year after surgery, which may have reduced the accuracy of assessing the true postoperative impact of AT. In addition, heterogeneity across included studies, particularly regarding patient populations, intervals between AT and postoperative PSG, and variability in AHI/OAHI thresholds used to define residual OSA, may have contributed to the wide range of reported prevalence rates and precluded quantitative meta-analysis. Therefore, the findings were synthesized using a structured narrative approach. A major strength of this review is its comprehensive and systematic approach, encompassing a broad spectrum of risk factors associated with rOSA. The findings clearly delineate subgroups of children who should undergo postoperative PSG assessment following AT and may meaningfully contribute to the development of future clinical guidelines. 5. Conclusions Residual OSA remains a clinically relevant concern in children after AT, although reported prevalence varies widely across studies due to heterogeneity in study design, definitions, and timing of postoperative assessment. The most consistent evidence supports an association between obesity, major comorbidities such as Down syndrome, and higher baseline OSA severity with increased rates of residual disease. Other factors, including craniofacial characteristics and socioeconomic or environmental determinants, have been reported in some studies but appear less consistently supported and should be interpreted cautiously. Given the heterogeneity across studies, careful postoperative assessment may be particularly relevant in higher-risk populations. documents.title: Efficacy and Safety of Hospital-at-Home versus Traditional Hospital Care in Older Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
documents.abstract:
Introduction: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of the Hospital-at-Home (HaH) model compared to traditional hospital care for older patients.
METHODS: We comprehensively searched PubMed, Embase, Medline, Cochrane Library, SinoMed, Scopus, and ClinicalTrials.gov for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published up to April 15, 2024. The primary outcomes were length of stay (LOS) and readmission rates. Secondary outcomes included total cost, mortality, adverse events, and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL).
RESULTS: Eleven RCTs involving 3,301 patients were included. The HaH group demonstrated a significantly shorter LOS (SMD = -0.45; 95% CI: -0.62 to -0.28; p < 0.01) and lower total healthcare costs (SMD = -0.40; 95% CI: -0.52 to -0.28; p < 0.0001) than the traditional care group. HaH was also associated with a reduced risk of readmission, with subgroup analyses showing consistent benefits at 1, 3, and 9 months. Additionally, patients receiving HaH showed modest but significant improvements in IADL scores (SMD = -0.15; 95% CI: -0.26 to -0.04; p < 0.0001). However, no significant differences were found between the two groups in terms of mortality (RR = 1.03; 95% CI: 0.49-2.18; p = 0.93) or adverse event rates (RR = 1.01; 95% CI: 0.43-2.36; p = 0.084).
CONCLUSION: For a selected group of older patients, HaH appears to be a viable alternative to traditional hospitalization, offering advantages in reducing LOS, healthcare costs, and readmission rates, while potentially improving functional recovery without increasing risks to patient safety. Further research is warranted to confirm these findings and refine implementation strategies. .

Exacerbated by bed shortages and workforce limitations, this strain compromises care quality and patient outcomes [ 4 , 5 ]. In response, innovative care models like Hospital-at-Home (HaH) have emerged as a critical alternative. HaH is a structured service model designed to deliver acute, hospital-level care as a substitutive alternative to traditional inpatient admission. It involves the active provision of comprehensive treatment by healthcare professionals (e.g., physicians, nurses, therapists) in the patient’s own home, typically including components such as remote monitoring, intravenous therapies, and scheduled visits. This model operates primarily through two pathways: admission avoidance (initiating care directly at home for eligible patients) and early discharge (facilitating continued hospital-level care at home following initial stabilization in the hospital) [ 6 , 7 ]. This model aligns with the preferences of many older patients to receive care at home and may reduce the risk of hospital-acquired complications [ 8 , 9 ]. While existing evidence suggests HaH can reduce costs and maintain care quality for selected acutely ill adults [ 10 , 11 ], its safety and efficacy for the more vulnerable older population – who are at higher risk of iatrogenic harm and functional decline – remain a subject of concern and incomplete understanding [ 12 ]. A comprehensive evaluation comparing HaH to traditional inpatient care for this demographic is therefore necessary. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate the efficacy and safety of HaH for older patients. We specifically examined critical outcomes including length of stay (LOS), readmission rates, total costs, mortality, and functional status (instrumental activities of daily living, IADL). This synthesis aims to provide a robust evidence base to guide clinicians and policymakers and to identify key areas for future research and model optimization. Methods This systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (registration number: CRD420251238936). Eligibility Criteria Population Older patients who were eligible for hospital care at home did not require ongoing acute hospital-based treatment (as judged by a consultant geriatrician) and consented to being treated at home. Older adults in this review were defined as individuals aged ≥65 years or studies where the proportion of older participants was more than 80%. This dual criterion was applied to include studies that primarily focused on an older population, even if the mean age was not explicitly above 65 years. We excluded adults under 50 years old and those residing in rehabilitation centers, nursing homes, or other healthcare facilities. Intervention The intervention group comprised patients eligible for HaH interventions, regardless of where they were assessed or treated. HaH interventions could admit patients directly from the community, avoiding hospital contact, or from the emergency room or an acute assessment unit. HaH was defined as a service model that provides active, hospital-level treatment by healthcare professionals in the patient’s home for conditions that would otherwise require acute inpatient care. This encompasses both admission avoidance models (where care is initiated directly at home) and early discharge models (where patients are stabilized in the hospital before transitioning home). The interventions typically involved a multidisciplinary team (e.g., physicians, nurses, physical therapists) and could include components such as remote vital signs monitoring, intravenous medication administration, and scheduled home visits. Comparator Only studies with control groups receiving care exclusively in hospital wards were included. Outcomes Primary outcomes included LOS and total cost. Secondary outcomes included mortality, readmission rates, adverse events, and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). Study Selection We included RCTs based on the implementation of the HaH model in older patients. HaH was defined as detailed above. Interventions delivered in outpatient settings, nursing institutions for the aged, or primarily involving patient self-care at home were excluded. Studies involving patients admitted due to worsening severe illness were also excluded. Search Strategy We conducted a comprehensive search of several major databases to identify relevant publications for our review. This included searching Web of Science (which encompasses the Web of Science Core Collection, MEDLINE, Embase, and the SciELO Citation Index), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, and EBSCO CINAHL Plus. Our search was conducted from the inception of these databases up until April 30, 2024. To ensure we captured all ongoing studies, we also searched ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. In addition to these database searches, we reviewed the reference lists of relevant Cochrane Reviews to identify any additional studies that might have been missed in our initial searches. The search strategy for PubMed is provided as an example: (“Hospital-at-Home” [Mesh] OR “HaH” OR “home hospitalization”) AND (“Aged” [Mesh] OR “elderly” OR “older adult”) AND (“Randomized Controlled Trial” [ptyp]). Similar strategies adapted to the syntax of each database were used and are available in the online supplementary Material S1 (for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000551394 ). Data Extraction To systematically collect and organize data from the included studies, we utilized a structured data extraction form. This form was designed to capture the following details. Participant Characteristics We recorded the title of the study, the name of the first author, the design of the study (such as RCT), and the publication time (year of publication). Basic Information of Study Subjects We documented the sample size of the study, the age range or mean age of the participants, the sex distribution, the type of disease or condition being studied, and the form of intervention being tested (such as medication, surgery, or behavioral therapy). Outcomes and Measures We extracted data on several key outcomes, including LOS, rates of readmission, total cost of care, mortality rates, and the level of independence as measured by instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). Data extraction was performed by two independent reviewers to ensure accuracy and minimize bias. In cases where there were disagreements between the two reviewers, these were resolved through discussion with a third reviewer to reach a consensus. Quality Appraisal Two independent researchers conducted a thorough evaluation of the quality of the studies that were included in the analysis. They utilized the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool [ 13 ], which is a well-established and widely recognized method for assessing the quality of research studies. This tool was specifically designed to evaluate various aspects of study design and conduct that could potentially introduce bias into the results. The researchers looked at several key components, including the methods used for random distribution of subjects, the concealment of allocation to ensure that the groups being compared were treated equally, the effectiveness of blinding procedures to prevent knowledge of group assignments from influencing the outcomes, the integrity of the data collected, and selective reporting, which refers to the practice of only reporting outcomes that are favorable to the hypothesis being tested. In addition to these, other sources of bias were also considered. Each study was then rated on a scale that indicated whether it had a low, high, or unclear risk of bias in these areas. To ensure the accuracy and consistency of the evaluations, any disagreements that arose between the two researchers were resolved through a collaborative discussion with a third independent reviewer. Data Synthesis and Reporting This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. The PRISMA 2020 checklist is provided as online supplementary Material S3. To evaluate the comparative effectiveness of hospital care at home versus traditional hospital care in older patients, we conducted comprehensive meta-analyses using Stata 18 statistical software (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). Continuous outcome measures were analyzed using mean differences with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs), while dichotomous outcomes were assessed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI. The presence and degree of heterogeneity across studies were systematically evaluated through the chi-square test (with statistical significance set at p < 0.10) and quantified using the I 2 statistic, which describes the percentage of total variation across studies attributable to heterogeneity rather than chance. Based on these assessments, we employed a fixed-effect model (Mantel-Haenszel method) when minimal heterogeneity was observed ( I 2 ≤ 50%), while a random-effects model (DerSimonian-Laird method) was utilized in cases of substantial heterogeneity ( I 2 > 50%) [ 14 ]. All statistical tests were two tailed, with the threshold for statistical significance established at α = 0.05. The results of these analyses were visually represented through forest plots, which provide a graphical display of effect estimates from individual studies along with their CI and the pooled estimate. Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of our findings by sequentially excluding each study and examining the impact on overall effect sizes. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test when more than 10 studies were available for a given outcome. Following a rigorous screening process, which involved the application of specific inclusion and exclusion criteria, 11 RCTs were ultimately selected for inclusion in our systematic review [ 9 – 12 , 15 – 21 ]. Risk of Bias The methodological quality of the 11 included RCTs was meticulously evaluated using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB 2.0). Nine studies showed a low risk of bias in random sequence generation (selection bias), reflecting proficient randomization procedures with appropriate methods like random number generators and tables, effectively mitigating selection bias. For allocation concealment (selection bias), six studies employed reliable techniques such as central randomization and sealed opaque envelopes to hide allocation sequences, preventing premature disclosure of group assignments and reducing bias. However, five studies lacked adequate concealment measures. In terms of blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias), ten studies were rated as low risk. Effective blinding strategies, including placebo controls, minimized bias stemming from awareness of intervention details. Similarly, for blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), ten studies showed low risk, indicating successful blinding of assessors to group allocations. Regarding incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), nine studies had a low-risk profile, suggesting proper handling of missing data, likely through methods like multiple imputation, with minimal impact on study outcomes. Nine studies also demonstrated low risk of selective reporting (reporting bias), fully reporting outcomes as per the study protocols. For other biases, eight studies showed no signs of additional bias, while three might have harbored unaccounted bias factors. Overall, the study series performed well across most bias domains, but allocation concealment required improvement to enhance overall quality and credibility. Still, with low bias risks in the majority of domains, the cumulative bias risk remained relatively low (see Fig. 2 for a summary of the risk of bias assessments). Primary Outcomes Length of Stay The pooled analysis of 9 RCTs revealed that HaH interventions significantly reduced length of hospitalization compared to conventional inpatient care. The random-effects model ( I 2 = 45%, p = 0.07) demonstrated a standardized mean difference (SMD) of −0.45 (95% CI: −0.62 to −0.28; p < 0.01), corresponding to an average reduction of 2.1 hospital days (95% CI: 1.3–2.9 days). The forest plot ( Fig. 3 ) illustrates consistent directionality of effects across studies. Sensitivity analysis showed robust results when excluding any single study (pooled SMD range: −0.41 to −0.49). Fig. 3. Egger’s test confirmed no small-study effects ( p = 0.21). Sensitivity analysis by sequentially removing each study did not significantly alter the pooled effect sizes for primary outcomes. Discussion Our synthesis indicates that the HaH model presents multiple benefits compared to traditional hospitalization for older patients. Our findings suggest that HaH may offer several advantages, including reduced LOS, lower healthcare costs, improved functional outcomes (IADL scores), and decreased readmission rates, without significantly compromising patient safety in terms of mortality or adverse events. Key Findings and Clinical Implications Shorter LOS and Reduced Costs A notable finding was the significantly reduced risk of readmission in the HaH group, particularly within the first month post-discharge. This aligns with the work of Shepperd [ 12 ]. The sustained reduction in readmissions at 3, 9, and 12 months further supports the hypothesis that home-based care may improve long-term disease management by enhancing patient adherence and reducing hospital-acquired complications. Furthermore, a more recent systematic review conducted by Lin et al. [ 22 ] has also found that HaH programs are indeed cost effective, especially for older adults who are experiencing acute exacerbations of chronic conditions. Our results serve to reinforce these previous observations, thereby suggesting that home-based care models can not only optimize resource utilization but also maintain clinical effectiveness. Lower Readmission Rates A notable finding was the reduced risk of readmission in the HaH group, particularly within the first month post-discharge. This aligns with the work of Shepperd [ 7 ], who found that early supported discharge programs significantly lowered 30-day readmission rates in older patients with heart failure and COPD. The sustained reduction in readmissions at 3, 9, and 12 months further supports the hypothesis that home-based care may improve long-term disease management by enhancing patient adherence and reducing hospital-acquired complications. However, our results contrast with some earlier studies [ 4 , 23 , 24 ], which reported no significant difference in readmission rates, possibly due to variations in patient selection and care coordination models. Functional Outcomes and Safety The improvement in IADL scores (SMD = −0.15) suggests that hospital care at home may better preserve or enhance functional independence in older patients, though the effect size is modest. This is in line with research by León-Muñoz et al. [ 25 ], who found that home-based rehabilitation led to greater improvements in daily living activities compared to inpatient care. However, the lack of significant differences in mortality and adverse events (e.g., falls, delirium) mirrors findings from a Cochrane review by Bruce [ 26 ], which concluded that while HaH is safe, it does not necessarily reduce mortality or severe adverse events compared to conventional hospitalization. The absence of significant differences in mortality and adverse event rates warrants further consideration. This finding may reflect the careful patient selection criteria employed in HaH programs, where only clinically stable patients with adequate home support are deemed eligible, thereby mitigating inherent risks. Furthermore, the intensive monitoring protocols, rapid response systems, and multidisciplinary support characteristic of many HaH models may effectively identify and manage complications early, offsetting potential safety disadvantages compared to the controlled hospital environment. The moderate heterogeneity and limited number of studies focusing on these hard safety endpoints suggest that larger, more homogenous trials are needed to definitively establish the safety equivalence or superiority of HaH. Relation to Other Studies Our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting HaH as a feasible alternative to traditional inpatient care. However, discrepancies with some prior studies highlight the importance of contextual factors such as patient selection, care model design, and healthcare system support. For instance, while our meta-analysis showed cost savings, a study by Levine et al. [ 21 ] found that savings were more pronounced in integrated healthcare systems with strong home-care infrastructure. Similarly, variations in readmission rates across studies may reflect differences in follow-up protocols and transitional care support. These inconsistencies suggest that the success of HaH programs depends on tailored implementation, including multidisciplinary team involvement, robust caregiver support, and seamless integration with primary care [ 27 – 30 ]. Future research should explore how specific program components (e.g., telehealth monitoring, intensity of nursing care) influence outcomes to guide best practices. Limitations and Future Directions Despite these promising results, our study has several limitations. First, the substantial heterogeneity observed in the analyses of readmission rates and costs ( I 2 > 90%) limits the generalizability of our pooled estimates. This heterogeneity likely stems from multiple sources, including fundamental differences in HaH operational models (admission avoidance versus early discharge), variability in healthcare system structures (e.g., funding, integration with primary care, availability of home-care resources), and diversity in patient populations (e.g., case mix, severity of illness, comorbidity burden). The variability in HaH components, as summarized in online supplementary Material S2, further underscores the challenge of comparing heterogeneous interventions. Second, the lack of standardized protocols across included trials complicates direct comparisons. Third, the geographical scope of the evidence is another consideration. The majority of included trials were conducted in Western, high-resource healthcare settings. The applicability of our findings to low- and middle-income countries or non-Western cultural contexts, where family caregiving dynamics, digital infrastructure, and health system integration differ substantially, remains uncertain. Future effectiveness trials in diverse socioeconomic and cultural environments are crucial. Fourth, while we assessed functional status via IADL, our analysis did not capture other critical patient-centered outcomes such as health-related quality of life, caregiver burden, or patient and family satisfaction. Incorporating these measures in future evaluations is essential for a holistic understanding of the value and impact of the HaH model on the lives of older adults and their support networks. Future research should focus on large-scale, multicenter RCTs with longer follow-up periods to assess sustainability of benefits. Additionally, exploring patient and caregiver satisfaction, as well as the impact of specific home-based interventions (e.g., telehealth, multidisciplinary teams), could provide deeper insights into optimizing this care model. Furthermore, our analysis focused on clinical and utilization outcomes. Future research should incorporate patient-reported outcomes and caregiver satisfaction to provide a more holistic evaluation of the HaH model’s value and impact on the quality of life. Conclusion In summary, HaH appears to be a viable alternative to traditional hospitalization for older patients, offering advantages in terms of LOS, cost-efficiency, readmission reduction, and functional recovery without increasing mortality or adverse event risks. However, given the heterogeneity and limitations of current evidence, further rigorous studies are needed to validate these findings and refine implementation strategies. Policymakers and healthcare providers should consider these results when designing and expanding HaH programs, particularly in aging populations with increasing healthcare demands.
